And then we move on in our text, and it tells us that we will find the will of God perfect. This is a huge concept this morning. We need to wrap our heads around this. God's will is perfect. As we face that this morning, we really have to do business with this. We need to take it to the wall, like Mike always did. Brad's name was recently drugged through the mud. The governor rescinded his position and maligned the job that he did in his line of work. Now, the question comes down to, is there some flaw in this? Was there some mistake in what happened that allowed this to happen to Brad? No. No, none. God's will is perfect. And what happened to Brad will serve as a tool in God's hand. To bring Brad to perfection, and who knows, maybe to bring other people to new life. We have no idea how God intends to use it But we can see how he has used it and we can see th the proper response to it. And Brad uh has been such an encouragement to me and an e example to follow in this situation that he has just gone through. So we we need to look at all of the things that happen from this perspective, from this sieve. And to see that God's will is truly perfect As we believe what God says about himself, as we believe what God says about his works, as we believe what God says about life events, we begin to understand, we begin to appreciate. That God's will is truly perfect. And not only is God's will perfect, his intention is to make his children perfect as well. Colossians 1, 27 and 28 says, To them God willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of his mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. Him we preach, warning every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus. The word for complete in this next text is also perfect. The same word. Hebrews 13, 20 and 21. Now may the God of peace who brought up our Lord Jesus from the dead, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant, make you complete. Perfect, in every good work to do his will, working in you what is well pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. And in the next passage the word for faultless is also the word perfect. Jude 1, 24 and 25. Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy. To God our Savior, who alone is wise, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and forever. Amen. That is what God has in mind for us. Perfection. And it will be given to us the moment we die. But we are working in that direction through our sanctification as we live. He is making us, heading us in that direction, preparing us for that final perfection that we will only attain. when we see him face to face. But that's what God has in mind for us, perfection. That is what Paul is telling us. That emphasizes his reasons for us to present our bodies as living sacrifices. To quit submitting ourselves to the world's pressures and to be transformed by the renewing of our minds. It is so that we can get the proper perspective on God's will, that we can see God for who he is and love him and appreciate him. That what he requests of us takes on a completely different light. We receive it from a God who loves us. And we recognize its value and we see its goodness. It's so that we can begin to really and totally experience God's will as truly being good and being for our good. We really need to ask ourselves, do we really experience what happens in our lives as God's will for our good? Then we will find it acceptable. Actually something that in essence smells good to us. The word for acceptable here was the same word that they talked about, the fragrance that came off of the offering to God. Do we really find ourselves glad to know that God is in charge of our life's situations? Do we face them as acceptable and pleasing from His hand? Do we see what God commands us to do as something that is pleasing to us? And then do we find them perfect? Do we really find them as the impeccable sovereign oversight to our lives? That is what is guaranteed. This is the growth that we will have as people. It is guaranteed if we will allow God to control the thoughts that go through our minds. That's what will happen if we'll quit allowing the world to tell us how to think and how to live and how to do anything. And we only think what God says. That's what will happen if we will only believe those things that God says are true to replace all the lies that we tend to pick up. I think we would do well to examine our reactions this week. Watch how you react when unpleasant things happen to you. What do you immediately think? What is the thought that follows that one? Where does it take you? Where do you end up? Does it send you into a spin? Or is it a bump in the road because you quickly reorient to the truth of God's word, to the orientation of God and His sovereign will over your life? As you're reading God's Word, how does your heart react to the commands that you read? Do you welcome them, or do you immediately resist them like you would a smell that you don't like? These are exactly the reactions that will change if we will simply submit to what God tells us to do, if we will present our bodies as living sacrifices. If we will stop being conformed to the world and its way of thinking, and if we will be transformed by the renewal of our minds. Let's close in prayer.

And if one believes that the application of Titus is universal, they would have to ask if the other children of the elder candidate are believers. Now, the question comes down. Since we're submitting to humans We must always submit with discernment. We must always obey God rather than man. And we must discern if the direction given by the authority is in the realm that the authority should have. But when it's proper, we must submit. And when we do not, it's no one's fault but ours. And more importantly, or maybe more clearly, does it show by how we submit to the authorities God has placed in our lives? Amen.

sermons.text: Last week we looked at what an elder should be. This week we'll look at a list of things an elder should not be. Verse 7, this is from the Titus text. Titus 1, verse 7, for a bishop must be blameless. As a steward of God, not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for money. Here we see the word blameless further defined as it applies to an elder. It's not just blameless about everything, it's blameless primarily with the list that he's going to go down. And first, the general framework of an elder is that he is a steward of God. A steward of God. An elder is dealing with valuable things that are not his own. And as such, he should deal with them as the owner would have them dealt with, not as he might just feel like dealing with them. Everything he does follows falls under this stewardship principle. His whole job is stewardship. There are many church leaders who get ambitious and want to make a name for themselves. They want to build something or accomplish something that puts their name in the spotlight They begin to see the body of people and the building those people meet in as their own personal items, their own personal church And when that happens, people will soon be sacrificed in order to meet goals and deadlines to fulfill this man's personal desires. The leaders can never afford to lose sight of the fact that while they are leaders, they are primarily servants Of those that they lead, and more still, they're servants of the head of the church, who is Christ, not who leaders serve. So an elder is always dealing with something of value that is owned by another. A man who acts like he is the head Who thinks of himself as the head, as think of thinks of himself as the church figurehead, is not fit to lead. He's gotta have a mindset of servanthood. The question could be asked of a potential elder, does this person live his life as if he believes he and the church Christ placed him in is owned by Christ and Christ alone? Then he goes on, not self-willed, not self-willed , not self-pleasing, self-willed or arrogant. He'll tell you what you should do to fit into his plans and ideas, rather than asking how he can help you to fit into God's. An elder should be a person that's willing to look after the needs of others at his own expense, following the model of Christ. He must show fleshly restraint and submission to the authority of God's Word. The question could be asked in this particular category. Does this man display a will that is submitted to the Word of God? Do you see evidence that the person must have his own way or will do it God's way at the expense of his own way? Not quick-tempered. Not quick-tempered. Prone to anger. Irascible. Prone to outbursts of temper. Easily angered. An elder cannot be a person that's easily out of control due to his anger. He must be able to think and reason and serve at any time. So an adequate question at as a result of This category would be: does this person use alcohol in such a way that it would interfere with him doing his job? Essentially, this word means a person ready for a fight. A person 's just always ready for a fight. A person with a chip on their shoulder. This is a person who is easily drawn into a fight. And an elder has to be holy It is very clear here that we must be talking about degrees. If the qualification for eldership was perfect holiness, Titus would have no candidates at all, nor would anyone else on this planet. But generally a person can be chosen who is living for Christ in such a way that he is not enslaved by any particular sins. Not living in an intentional pattern of sin, and in general is obeying Christ in his day-to-day life I think that's more in line with what is meant here, what is intended, what is uh uh actually achievable This kind of holiness represents genuine faith. So an elder is responsible first to pay attention to his own life, but it doesn't end there He must also pay attention to those in the body, and even starting with the group of elders. Everyone in the body is told to do this as well. So that's a good thing. We have help. We're to look out for one another, but the elders have the ultimate responsibility. At the end of the day, the elders must look out after the flock. Notice that these words are put in shepherding terms. And that isn't unusual at all. Elders need to view their responsibility in those kinds of terms. We're given the charge to take care of another person's property. These sheep are precious to the owner, and an elder has to treat them appropriately, knowing that. So elders are to intentionally look out for the good of everyone under their care. They must have an intentional focus. Then he goes on to say, Among which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Now this is interesting. In Timothy, it says it's good for a man to want this position and to pursue it. In Titus, Titus is told to appoint these guys. But here we see that the real truth of the matter goes deeper than all of that. Ultimately, it is the Holy Spirit who makes a man an overseer. A man may have decided he wanted to be an elder, another may have appointed him to be an elder, but at the end of the day, it's the Holy Spirit who appoints men to be leaders in the church It's a very serious, a very weighty appointment. And the word for overseer means just that. A person charged with the duty of seeing that things to be done by others are done rightly. Also of one who watches over others. Like a shepherd. You know, it it the shepherding illustration really carries a depth of understanding simply in the word that's used. So it's it's really helpful And he goes right on, has made you overseers for what? To shepherd the church of God, which he purchased with his own blood. I really like that word shepherd. I gather you can probably get that. It conveys so much with one word. Christ is the good shepherd, the over -shepherd, the master shepherd. All those words are used of him. All an elder needs to do is to look how Christ shepherded his flock, and we'll know much of what we need to know. He serves as our perfect example. In the culture which this was written in, it would be easy to understand what a shepherd did. He would be placed in an area where he would see that the sheep had everything that they needed. Of first importance, the sheep had to have food. So the shepherd would lead them to new sources of food daily Then the sheep also had to have water, so he would lead them to water. Third, they needed tended for any sicknesses or injuries. And fourth, they needed protection from wolves. That's what elders are responsible for doing. Same thing. And we're doing all those things because the sheep belong to Christ, and Christ values the sheep. Christ purchased the sheep with his own blood, our passage tells us. He owns them. That's what gives the sheep their value. That is why we are valuable Christ loves us. It's certainly not the wonderful goodness that we bring to this picnic. It's him. It's the value that Christ placed on us. The shepherd knows that the sheep are not likely to look out for the shepherds. At least the good shepherd does. It'd take a pretty much of an idiot of a shepherd to think that it was going to work out the other way. So they're not surprised when they're not treated by the sheep as they would prefer. Basically, the shepherds are there for the good of the sheep, not the other way around. Now, the analogy falls apart because in the church we're all to love one another. I, as an elder, have certainly been loved by you, and I greatly appreciate that. But what I'm trying to say is that if there is w if one is to be an elder, that person must understand it is a position that demands self-sacrifice. This is not like a position at work where the position comes with some prestige or money or power. No, in the church position, it comes with more work and more sacrifice. A person who is called to be an elder must understand that. Now, Paul tells the elders at his meeting what's to come to the Ephesian church And he'll share why it's important that they take their job seriously. Verse 29, he says, For I know that after my departure Savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock. Also, from among yourselves men will rise up, speaking perverse things to draw away the disciples after themselves. Wolves. Wolves. Wolves were one of the greatest dangers to the flock of sheep. And the only way a flock could survive is if the shepherd did his job against the wolves. The wolf the the sheep had no protection. Well there are still spiritual wolves. They're armed with doctrines spawned by demons. That's how Scripture describes it. It's that despicable. And the wolves still try to divide and conquer. They replace truth with carefully crafted lies. And once believed, the lies spread, and the more they spread, the more they destroy. Now, look where the wolves come from. Inside the flock and outside the flock. And what will they do? How will you know they're wolves and not sheep? By what they speak. And what do these wolves speak? Perverse things. They distort the true and the good into something that it should not be. They convince people to turn away from the right path. They plot against the saving purposes and plans of God. They distort truth. These elders are expected to be first, be able to show the error of these false teachers. And second, they're expected to do whatever's necessary to stop them from doing harm to the flock. So they've got to first recognize it and second act to stop it Essentially, any elder must understand that he is called into a position where confrontation and conflict are expected. If a man is afraid of conflict, he should not be an elder. Nothing should be more fierce than a shepherd protecting a flock. Now, Paul reminds these men what shepherding looks like. They had seen it firsthand, so they have no excuse to pretend that they don't know what it looks like. Verse 31. Therefore watch and remember that for three years I did not cease to warn everyone night and day with tears. That's what good eldering looks like. Work. Work. Remember in Acts how Paul would work through the hottest part of the day preaching and teaching? Because that was probably the only part of the day available to him and his people That's what good eldering looks like. It means doing whatever needs done to see that the sheep are fed and protected. It means putting aside our comfort for their welfare. Verse 32. So now, brethren, I command you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified. Paul's finishing up. He commends them to God. It's like he is handing them off to God for it for God to finish them off. Finish them up. And he emphasizes what thing God will use to accomplish what needs done. And the thing that God will use is the word of God's grace. Essentially, that's the gospel. It's God's word that will enable these men to do the job that they're called to do It is that, when accompanied by the Spirit of God, that can build up an elder into being a good elder. And look at the encouragement he gives. It's the same word that gives us an inheritance. Oh, the wonder of it. We're going to get a rich portion of that which our Father has. That's true of all believers. But instead of getting it when he dies, we get it when we die. Brothers and sisters, this isn't limited to elders. This is for every believer. Are you facing some hard times? Is it hard going for you? Find hope in this. It's not always going to be this way. There is a fixed and certain end to it, and we will receive a rich reward. It's guaranteed by God. So you can hang your hope on that, and your hope is well placed Paul goes on and tells more of the qualities that he showed that make make them a good shepherd, and made him a good shepherd. Verse 33, I have coveted no one silver or gold or apparel. No coveting. Being an elder is not a way to get stuff that other people have. An elder must guard against any kind of coveting and nip it in the bud when it shows up, because an elder has influence. And it would be easy and awful for an elder to use that influence for selfish gain. Verse 34. Yes, you yourselves know that these hands have provided for my necessities and for those who were with me. I have shown you in every way by laboring like this that you must support the weak. No freeloading. Paul was a workhorse. He even provided an income for himself and his fellow workers that he would have not needed to. He holds this up as an example for the attitude that men who are elders should have. That which we have is to be used for those who do not have. Our strength should be used to take care of the weak, is essentially the principle here. I suspect that Paul was saying all this because these men were beginning to get the wrong idea. The world was creeping into their mindset. They were beginning to see their positions as a means to get things for themselves. Paul's laying it out in no uncertain terms here. Leadership in Christ Church means service. Elders are not there to get a benefit, they are there to give a benefit. And he goes on. And remember the words of the Lord Jesus that he said that it's more blessed to give than to receive. This statement is true for every believer, but it becomes even more important for leadership. There's a sense of entitlement in every man. We all experience it all the time. We feel that we should have a special exception to the rule. We might think that this is how everybody ought to live But when we want to live a different way, we can always find a reason why we're kind of special. We shouldn't have to live according to the standard that we preach. That sense says that I have some privilege because after all I am special in some way. And that is particularly dangerous when chosen to serve as a leader Christ gave us the proper perspective. Have you ever noticed that you experience your worth more when you give than when you get? We tend to think that getting will make us happy. But it rarely does. You ever notice? You know As kids, you know, you look forward to Christmas, you look forward two days later, all those toys, they don't give you a thrill anymore. And and even when they do, it's pretty temporary and it's real fleeting. It's not satisfying. But oddly enough, when we give, we're enriched. We usually even feel better. I mean it even works out in the here and now. And we find that people become more dependent upon us, and we find that they need us and they even want us around, which I don't know about you guys, but in my case was pretty remarkable. That was when that started happening, I went, how did that happen? Wow, this is pretty cool. Think about it. Who wants to be around the person who's always looking for their own angle? Who's always looking to get, but never looking to give. Even relationally, we can see that there's no blessing in being a getter. An elder is called to a giving position. He must understand that. It's a blessed position for sure, but not in what it will get for itself, but in what it will provide for others. Next we see what a a giving life produces in verses 36 -37. And when he had said all these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all, and they all wept freely and fell on Paul's neck and kissed him. sorrowing most of all for the words which he spoke, that they would see his face no more. Here is the elder 's earthly reward. Here is Paul's earthly reward. It doesn't always work out this way, but most people over time who love Christ understand the value of being shepherded. They become dependent upon those who are there for them, looking out for them, praying for them, being with them, and protecting them. These men loved Paul, and losing him from their lives was a considerable loss. That is the normal result of an elder loving his flock. Much of the time his flock loves them back. Now let's look at one more passage on eldering, and this one's much shorter. In 1 Peter 5, 1 through 4 First Peter five, one through four. The elders who are among you I exhort, I who am a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ. Notice too, Paul is a fellow elder. Uh oh no, I'm sorry, it was Peter Never mind. And also a partaker of the glory that will be revealed. Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, serving as overseers not by compulsion, but willingly. Not for dishonest gain, but eagerly, nor as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock And when the chief shepherd, see, chief shepherd appears, you'll receive the crown of glory that does not fade away. Here we have leadership guidance by Peter. He's saying much the same thing as Paul said. Shepherd the flock. Shepherd the flock. We have the same attitude, the same words, the same focus. And the elders are to realize just who they are shepherding. They are the flock of God Those are sheep that God deeply loves. That's what makes them important. Not by compulsion, but willingly. This is not a position a man should take grudgingly or half-heartedly. He shouldn't take it out of some sense of obligation. He should take it because he wants to serve Christ in this manner. The service he does should be this kind of service. Now, we might all have our own style of flushing this out and thinking it through and coming to that conclusion. It might not all look like, yeah, rah-rah, boy, I can't wait to do this. But it's that mentality behind it says, I want to serve Christ this way. He has done so much for me, this is the least that I can do in his service. But if a man is to be an elder, he's got to be all in. It's a big deal. Then he goes on to say, not for dishonest gain, but eagerly. Again, an elder can't go into the position for the wrong reason. He's got to go into it for the right reason. To pilfer the church accounts, not a good reason. But to serve Christ, good reason. Verse 3, nor as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. Here's another bad reason to be an elder. Some people just like telling other people what to do. They like having power over another person's life. That's not eldering. Sheep wouldn't last long under a leader like that. No, an elder must be an example of service, not of egotism and self-centeredness. We must be the chief servants. We must be examples of being willing to do whatever it takes to see that this sheep thrive. Now, none of us can do everything. We need to share the load. But we need to be careful in what we delegate, or we can begin acting like worldly lords, the worldly bosses We as elders, or really as any position in authority, should not delegate our tasks to others simply because we don't want to do them. We need to determine which of the tasks we can do and should do. They aren't all the tasks, but the ones that we can do and should do, we should do. If there are some that we should not do, or another should do, that's what we should delegate. In all of this, we can see that there's no self-centered reason for anyone to be an elder. That's essentially what we learn here. There's no good selfish reason to be an elder. But we should not get the impression that there's no reward, because there is a reward. There's no reward promised in this life for this job. Inevitably, there'll be some reward in terms of the love and appreciation we sometimes receive from others. For the work that we perform, that's normal, not promised, but it's normal, not guaranteed. There is, however, a guaranteed reward. For the work that we do as elders. Verse 4. And when the chief shepherd appears, when the big boss arrives. When Christ comes, you will receive the crown of glory that does not fade away The only reward promised for doing the work of an elder is from Christ's hand and it lasts forever. Christ will make it worthwhile for any man who is willing to diligently serve his church as an elder. And that is a good reason. A self Self-interested reason for doing this work. I just want to read one more scripture in closing, and it adds a picture of just what elders are sometimes up against. and why their work is so important. This is from Titus immediately after giving the qualifications of an elder. Titus 1 and 10 through 16 For there are many insubordinate, both idle talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, whose mouths must be stopped who subvert whole households, teaching things they ought not, for the sake of dishonest gain. And one of them, a prophet of their own, said, Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, and lazy gluttons. Paul wasn't very politically correct. This this testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply that they may be sound in the faith, and that sharply is no small thing. Not giving heed to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn from the truth. To the pure all things are pure, but to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. But even their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess to know God. But in works they deny him, being abominable, disobedient, and disqualified for every good work That is a problem for an elder. That is a job for an elder. Elders will be called upon to do things that are very difficult. Very uncomfortable and sometimes very risky. They're responsible for everything that happens in the church, and they are absolutely necessary. They have a job to do, and they must do their job. That's the scriptural proposition

sermons.title: What Legalism Always Accomplishes
sermons.speaker: Jon Zeigler
sermons.text: Well , this wor week we return to the book of Mark. We've been to church camp and we learned about killing sin, which is a logical application of the gospel of Christ in our day-to-day lives. Then for two weeks we looked at the qualifications of an elder, and the third week we looked at the job of an elder We're in the middle of appointing two elders in training, and we've ridden the roller coaster of dealing with regulations in the building of our meeting place. So that's that's where we're at. I think it would be good to remind ourselves where we are in the context of Mark to catch up. It's been a while We had read about Jesus telling his men that they were headed for a restful spot. When they got there, the disciples learned there was work to be done. It was a teaching time for them. Afterward, they were sent across a lake only to face a deadly storm, and Jesus arranged to act as if he were going to stroll past them in the middle of the lake. It had a dramatic effect on the disciples, and it turned the corner for them on realizing just who Christ was. When they reached their destination, miraculously and instantaneously, Jesus began teaching the crowds the next day. He talked to them about the two kinds of bread seekers. Most of the crowd rejected him at this point, proving that they were seeking the wrong bread. And now we come to our text in verse 1. Then the Pharisees and some of the scribes came together, having come from Jerusalem. We already know that the religious leaders in Jerusalem want Christ dead. That is their stated purpose. That's their goal, and everything that they do is in that regard. Another gospel tells us that Jesus was ministering in Galilee during this time because those who were in Judea wanted to kill him. It was a bit safer in Galilee. They at least had to travel farther. Jesus is going to use the next seven months to train his disciples out of out of the main thoroughfare in Judea. So these religious leaders approach Christ from a distance. We can assume that there is nothing sincere in anything that they do. When a person seeks to harm you, you don't need to play games with that fact. You don't need to assume that all their questions are sincere. Christ knew what these men were coming from, where they were coming from. He knew their hearts, and he's not about to put up with any of their nonsense. Verse 2. Now when they saw some of his disciples eat bread with defiled, that is, unwashed hands, they found fault. I think probably all of us here know. When people are looking for fault, you can rest assured that they're always going to find it, real or otherwise. In Christ's instance, it was always otherwise. For us, sometimes it's legitimate When the Jews came back from Babylonian captivity, they came back with an oral tradition of rules. Eventually, these rules were written in the Mishnah. Along with them were added rabbis' commentaries called the Gemara. The combination is called the Talmud. The Talmud basically says that God appointed men by the oral law that Moses passed down to create laws in order to protect God's written law or to aid in God's written law. These created laws were originally probably well-intended rules for helping people obey God's law. But the original intention doesn't really matter. We'll see some universal problems of legalism that's displayed in our text this morning. Any man-made rule that pretends to have the same authority as a God-made rule will, by its very nature, be used for evil. Any man-made rule that pretends to have the same authority as a God-made rule will by its very nature be used for evil. Any man-made rule that pretends to have the same authority as a God-made rule will eventually supersede God's rule. It will eventually supersede God's rule Any man-made rule that pretends to have the same authority as a God-made rule will eventually be used to punish and exclude those who care most about God's rule. It will eventually be used to punish and exclude those who care most about God's rule. Any man-made rule that pretends to have the same authority as a God-made rule will be used in a process of rejecting the authority of God. It will be used in a process of rejecting the authority of God And any man-made rule that pretends to have the same authority as a God-made rule will soon be used to evaluate spiritual success or failure. It will soon be used to evaluate spiritual success or failure. These are universal truths. We'll see them all through Scripture. And where such rules exist in churches today, we'll see the same thing. Legalism is the process of adding rules to God's directives. Usually in an attempt to help one live up to God's directives. But it never works. And it always leads to distraction of God's directives. For us to do such a thing in our own lives is absolutely necessary. But for us to do it to other believers is somewhere between foolish and evil. The religious leaders pointed out a problem. The disciples were eating without washing their hands. Now, this isn't in the order of what your mother did when you showed up for lunch from playing outside with dirty hands. This was something, this wasn't something for your health. This was a ceremonial cleansing. It wasn't so much intended to wash off germs. as it was to wash off any contact you may have had with something that was ceremonially unclean. Maybe somebody you touched was an unclean Gentile Maybe that person had touched or eaten pork. Maybe they had been around any number of unclean situations. This rule was designed to ceremonially get rid of that impurity. This was not something that the common people were required by Old Testament law to do. The priests had to wash, but the common people did not. But the Mishnah required the common person to ceremonially wash their hands before eating. This is a description of the ceremony from John MacArthur's commentary. First, water was poured from a jar onto both hands with the fingers pointing up, so you would kind of go like that, so that the water would run off at your wrists. And then water was again poured over the hands with your fingers pointing down. Finally, each hand was rubbed with the fist of the other hand. And strict Jews would follow these regulations before every meal and between each course in the meal. It's not difficult to imagine the discussion and the thinking that was carried on to come up with such a rule. Maybe it started with the concern that Hey, our young people are not getting the importance of remaining ceremonially unclean. And we all as good Jews know how important that is, and they're not getting it. They're forgetting what a big deal that is. We need to help them. Let's see. How can we do that? Oh, I know. Let's make them wash their hands. That way they'll be reminded of uncleanness that surrounds them. Good idea. But when? Well, how about when they eat? First, everyone wants to eat and has to eat, and if we couple it with eating, we can be sure that they get this important lesson about purity. Yes, and people probably won't do it unless we tell them that it's required. So let's make it so. Let's make it so that if you really want to worship God, well, you must do this before you eat. This will help our people to live godly lives. Can you see how that stuff starts? It looks good. It looks helpful. But what it does is shows a mistrust in the wisdom of God. If God wanted this in Scripture, it would be in Scripture. I think all of us have ideas of what should be in Scripture, but it isn't. There are any number of ways we think we should help God out here. But God doesn't need the help. He gave us his word, and that is exactly what he wants it to be. We do very well to limit ourselves to what he said And we all need to apply it to our lives with whatever legalism is necessary for us to obey God. But we must never think that others are required to go by our own personal legalisms. If I think it's wrong for me to have a cable TV because I'll waste too much time, that does not mean it's wrong for someone else to purchase that same thing. If someone wants to drink alcohol because of , or they don't want to drink it because of the harm that it may do to them, that does not mean that someone else must abstain. What the religious leaders did in Babylon displayed a mistrust of God and his word. And in the end, they did a great disservice to God. by passing down rules that would eventually become weapons to use against the true people of God. Mark goes on to tell us more about these Mishnah legalisms. He said in ver- says in verse 3, For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands in a special way, holding the tradition of the elders. When they come from the marketplace, they don't eat unless they wash. And there are many other things which they have received and hold as having authority, like the washing of cups, pitchers, copper vessels, and couches. Couches is left off on the most accurate translations. So we find lots of rules about lots of things. That's always what happens when we make little compromises with the purity of God's Word. It always leads to more and more compromises, more and more ways we think to help God out And the one thing you can trust about a legalist, they'll always view it as a fighting offense if you don't comply to their mutually accepted rules. They want conformity more than anything. We see that in the Pharisees' next question, in verse 5. Then the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with unwashed hands? Now, this could have been asked by a sincere person with a sincere longing to know, but that was not the case here. These people wanted to kill Christ. So we can assume their evil motives in asking the question. In essence, it was like so many insincere questions. It is really an accusation, not a question. It isn't like Christ could give them an answer that would satisfy them. There was nothing that Christ could say that would satisfy them. They would just move on to the next thing, the next opportunity. And the issue really isn't with what the disciples are doing. The leaders could have asked the disciples, but they didn't. No, the issue is about Jesus as the teacher of those disciples. The problem they're addressing is what Jesus is teaching his followers. That's what they're after with their insincere questions. We can read this assuming that the Pharisees were really saying, what they were really saying was, Jesus, you are blatantly teaching your disciples to sin in regard to ceremonial washings. You are challenging the whole structure of the Jewish traditions. That's what they're after. Verse 6: He answered and said to them, Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites? As it is written, This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. And in vain they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. For laying aside the commandment of God, you hold the tradition of men, the washing of pitchers and cups and many other such things you do. Jesus is not going to play a game with these men. He's not going to pretend that there is a speck of legitimacy in what these men are doing. He immediately calls them hypocrites. The word means play actor. We've gone over this a lot of times. They are one person while holding up an actor's face representing something completely different. Not at all congruent with the person behind the mask. These men were God haters and self-lovers. They loved what religion provided for them, but they could care less about anybody else. Yet they were talking to Jesus in the pretense of protecting true religion. Protecting true worship of God. It's difficult to imagine any act that would have been more hypocritical. But isn't that danger always with us too? How about when we don't like what somebody else is doing? Maybe we're secretly envious or jealous. Maybe we wish our conscience would allow us to do that thing that someone else is doing. Maybe it personally offends us simply because we find it distasteful. We can have all kinds of motives, but we approach the person or talk about the person like we have nothing but the purest spiritual motives for that person's welfare. We need to learn to spot this deadly seed. It's nothing but hypocrisy, pure and simple. When flesh is the secret motivation for us to confront a brother or a sister, that is one of the most harmful forms of hypocrisy. Before you talk about a brother or sister or confront a brother or sister, ask yourself this question. Is my true goal in my heart of hearts For this person to experience the peace and the blessing of God. Is that my goal? Or is there a motive of punishment or retribution? Our hearts really are despicable. And they're often most despicable when we pretend to care about God and about the other person. Jesus told his questioners that they were the perfect examples of what Isaiah the prophet wrote. They could pretty well quote, they pretty well knew from the start that this was not about to be complimentary. These guys knew this scripture. Then Jesus quoted Isaiah 29, 13, This people honors me with their lips. But their heart is far from me. And in vain they worship me, teaching his doctrines, the commandments of men. For laying aside the commandment of God, you hold the tradition of men, the washing of pitchers and cups. Jeremiah's first statement is the definition of spiritual hypocrisy. I believe that was Jeremiah 29, 13. Not sure then. They wear the mask of honoring God, worshiping God, caring about God's glory. Yes, the mask is all about God. The mask is very godly. The stated purpose with their lips is that they're all about God. They're all about spiritual things. That's all they care about. Yep. Their lips say the right things. They have the external all worked out. They give the proper impressions. They say and do the right things externally. But they have a huge problem, a huge disconnect, a huge hypocrisy. Their hearts and their words don't line up. They're actually at odds with each other. When our lips are saying things that don't represent our hearts, that is hypocrisy. When we posture having spiritually loving motives, but we really have very different motives, very fleshly motives. That is hypocrisy at its worst. True worship is the congruence of heart and lips. True worship is when our hearts truly want to please God and our lips are an expression of that truth. We can know when that's true because we care little about how it's perceived. We don't have to work to appear a certain way or have to have to have people approve of what we're doing or saying. We're doing it as unto the Lord, and we know the Lord is watching, and we answer to him, and it's all good We don't have to worry about how we're perceived. Congruence of life and heart is what a Christian shoots for. We're the only people who are free to live in truth. We don't have to hide. We don't have to pretend. Christians are set free to be what they are. And when we see that we're incongruent, we at that point can confess it and be real with it. It's not like we're going to get kicked out of the club. That's what grace is all about. That's how we got in. We didn't get in by getting by being by being good. We didn't get in by pretending anything. We got in by pretend or by receiving what Christ gave to us. And that's how we stay in. So we can give up that battle. We can give up that farce. We don't have to act. We can be who we are. Granted, that's not always good, and it requires a lot of change, but we can be who we are. Now, next Isaiah, after defining hypocrisy, tells us the point of failure. He says, in vain they worship me. In vain they worship me. These incongruent people are trying to worship God, but they have not started where true worship always starts. True worship always starts in humility and repentance. It's seeing God for who God is and realizing by default who we are. It starts with our hearts adjusting to who God is and who we are. It tells the truth to God and accepts the truth from God. But religious people attempt to worship God as they are. In their pride, they approach God seeking to do something for him, to do him a favor. And they'll always find that all their efforts of worship are in vain. They'll think they're doing something that pleases God and helps God, but they're always wrong. Their efforts will produce nothing with God. Now, how are this particular people thinking to help God, thinking to worship God? Teaching as doctrines, the commandments of man. That's how they were helping God. Are we ashamed of Christ and denying Christ? I think we would do well to answer those questions in ways that we are certain of. To look at our lives and see, I know that my life is being lived for Christ. It's not being lived perfectly, but I know that it is. Or we look at it and say, you know. There is no difference between me and the people who are walking down the street. My life looks just the same. I just claim a Christianity that has no power over my life. I'm not denying my my life. We need to examine it Living for Christ isn't always going to look a specific way, but we know what it is in our life that is different because we're dedicated to Him. But that you showed your worth, but your value, your holiness And that it is worth following you, being yours, being in relationship with you, is worth more than this world could ever offer us. We ask that you would help us in our pursuit of following you, and as we examine our lives, that we would see the truth About whether we are yours or whether we are not, and then about how we could live in such a way that would more please you, that would more further your cause. That would accomplish more for your kingdom, that would reward us even more in your eternal kingdom. And that we would consider your worth in all of this. And to know that you are worthy to receive glory, honor, and power forever. Amen.

sermons.text: And he said to them, Assuredly, I say to you, that there are some standing here who will not taste death till they see the kingdom of God present with power. This is a difficult passage, with the million-dollar question being: what is the kingdom of God present with power? What is it that Christ was referring to? Well, we have some clues. sermons.title: The Problem with Idolatry
sermons.speaker: Jon Zeigler
sermons.text: So a few weeks ago we looked at the Rich Young ruler and we saw that he was loaded with potential. What a ministry opportunity. But all of it was a loss when all that potential kept him from eternal life. Then our last sermon was on what Jesus meant when he said that the last shall be first and the first shall be last, and we looked at the parable of the hiring of the laborers. Now, back in Mark 10 in verse 23, we pick up where we left off in the story of the rich young ruler. Jesus wants to give his disciples insight on the topic of what just happened. And what he teaches turns the disciples' mental constructs about life upside down. The rich young ruler had just left with all the wind taken out of his sails. He was asked to give up his idol that he worshipped, and he refused. There is little that will make you more miserable than refusing to give up that which you love more than God. There is little that will make you more miserable than refusing to give up that which you love more than God. Is there anything like that in our lives? If this had been us instead of the rich young ruler, what would Christ have told us that we should get rid of and follow him? Is there anything that we would say no to if we knew that it was God who was asking the question? If there is, that thing, by its very definition, is an idol. Notice that the thing that the rich young ruler held on to was not forbidden by the law. It was permissible. It wasn't expedient, but it was permissible. No one could have shown this guy a scripture and said, you must sell this stuff But even though it was not forbidden for this guy, it was not allowable. Many of the issues in our lives are like this. If we can't thank God for it, if we can't enjoy it in our fellowship with God, it may be something we should rid ourselves of, even though it may be technically permissible. What idol do you have in your life this morning? What do you hold on to tighter than God? That tends to be the sin that God gives the most ink to in Scripture, idolatry, because it's offensive to him and it's dangerous to us. Now let's look at what Jesus says about wealth. Verse 23, then Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, How hard it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God. The Jews had a book of teachings called the Talmud. The Talmud taught that with wealth one could purchase more sacrifice and give more alms. There was a basic understanding that by doing those things, one gained salvation for oneself. The more money you had, essentially, the better salvation you could buy. So Jews were taught that wealth was a desirable goal, even a necessary goal if you really wanted to please God. And it was also understood that wealth was a blessing from God. So if you ask any Jew, will possession of money be a sign of God's approval on you? And a tool to win God's approval of you, most Jews would have said yes. What possession must you have before you will be happy? How much money must you have before you can be content? If the answer isn't, I have all I need , I'm content. Odds are that no amount of possessions will ever make you happy. You'll be just like that rat on the spinning wheel. That desire is fleeting. Look what Paul says about it. But those who desire to be rich desire to have more, they never have enough. They fall into a temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. For which some have strayed from the faith in their greediness and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. Trying to get rich and trying to stay rich are both dangerous things Paul says that this desire to always have more ends up trapping a person. When we cling to the longing of that which we wish we had. We will find that longing will pierce us through with many unnecessary sorrows. Know therefore and understand that from the going forth of the command to restore and build Jerusalem Until Messiah the Prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. The street shall be built again and the wall, even in troublesome times After the sixty-two weeks, Messiah shall be cut off, but not for himself, and the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end of it shall be with a flood, and till the end of the war, desolations are determined. So in the prophecy in Daniel, each week was seven years. So 7 weeks plus 62 weeks equals 69 weeks. 69 weeks times seven years equals 483 years. And so there were 483 years from Artaxerxes' decree until Christ entered the city. So when Christ entered the city, he fulfilled this important expectation that the Messiah would truly enter Jerusalem in the year in which Christ did. And people knew that. That's why some of them knew that Christ had to be born. They knew that he had to exist right then. This entry was very important in God's timetable. It had to happen. And it did. And then verse eleven. And Jesus went into Jerusalem and into the temple. So when he had looked around at all things, as the hour was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. It must have taken a long time for Christ to ride this donkey through the songing crowd. Maybe all day. It's not that great of a distance. It's less than a mile. When he was done with the ride, he went into the city and into the temple and he observed everything. The city was his, after all. Christ was preparing for the upcoming week This was the first day of his final week in Jerusalem. Once he got the lay of the land, he went back out of the city, probably to stay with Mary, Martha, and Lazarus at Bethany. So in closing, there's a question we should look at. Jesus allowed the people to openly praise and worship him. In the past he had stopped much of this activity, but now he allows it. Why? Why would that be? Well, if we go with the theory that we've taken so far from the clues of what Jesus has said, if Jesus had stopped it in the past because if it would have led to his death, prior to his planned time, then it makes perfect sense that he allows the crowd to praise him now. His time's up It's now time to die. So he is now willing to accept the praise that he deserved all along. Also, it was important that Christ be slain on Passover as the Passover lamb So Christ may have been using the crowd and the Jewish leader's hatred of Christ and the greed of Judas to make sure that he died at the correct time. From our perspective, doesn't it look like all these things happened to Christ? Doesn't it just look like, well, people made this decision and people made that decision and Judas made this decision and it just happened? But from God's perspective, he had everything planned to the minute. All the players were responsible. For what they did in this play. Every one of them are going to be found guilty for the part that they played. But someone was going to play that part. How all that works out is beyond the realm of human reason. We don't get it, we can't get it, we're not going to get it. But we can rest assured that it does work out. I think a final good application for us this morning is this. We can find great comfort In the sovereignty and omniscience and omnipotence of God Look at this event in our text. There were thousands of things that had to be in place for this week to accomplish what was in God's mind. Christ had to step foot into Jerusalem on a distinct date of the calendar. The Jews had to be prepared to kill him. There had to be a betrayer ready to betray him on that date, in that hour, as a matter of fact. There had to be an unridden donkey available in a nearby town. And it goes on and on. But none of this was hard to God. And none of it was simply at the whim of what a person might choose to do. It was perfectly planned, even using humans who have choices. Variables that we would see as impossible to know or certainly to plan. Our lives rest in this same sovereign God's hand. His plans for us are good. He causes all things to work out for the good for those who love him, those who are of the called. If our hearts and minds tell us that our lives are out of God's control, our hearts and minds are lying to us. It only seems that way. God has a plan and he will fulfill it for his children. There is no person or no event that can interfere with that. Do you trust God? Do you trust God with your life? Do you trust that he is applying his sovereign rule to the plan that he has for your life no matter how it looks right now? If you are his, that is what he promises. Let's close in prayer Lord, we thank you. We come before you befuddled. We can't imagine why. You would do that for us. We know us. And we can only ascribe it To an amazing love. Amazing love that we can't can't relate to We can only receive it as it's been revealed. We praise you For this sovereignty that you display being worked out for our good Help us to believe that when our hearts and minds want to scream out that it's not so, when we interpret the evidence through our flesh and say that it can't be. When we tell you how things should be, instead of coming to you with how they are Help us, Lord, to rest in your sovereignty, to know where peace really is found. And to be crying out the save us that matters for eternity. Help us to be those kind of people and to receive your loving kindness and trust in it every hour. In Jesus name, amen

sermons.text: Remember last week's text? Jesus entered the city in what appeared to be a triumphal entry, but in reality it was just another expression of flesh by the crowd. They wanted Jesus to be what they wanted him to be, and when they found out that he wasn't here to fulfill their role, their exuberance in praising him turned into rage in hating him. Once in Jerusalem, Jesus went in and took a look around, and then he turned away and went back to Bethany, probably to stay with Mary, Martha, and Lazarus for the night. The text this morning will tell us about the next day. Verse 12. Now the next day when they had come out from Bethany, he was hungry. Jesus was hungry. So Jesus and his disciples are making the trek back to Jerusalem, this time evidently not with such a throng of crowd. It wasn't very far, and Jesus was hungry. Now, this isn't a big point, but then again, maybe it is. Surely He will not hold it against me in this instance if I do it. It's too hard for me. I can't overcome these creature desires. So what I read on this was that this is an unusual tree. Normally leaves and figs would come out at the same time. So if it had leaves, it had figs. If it had figs, it had leaves. So normally if a fig tree had the leaves, it would also have the figs. And not only that, this tree was about a month ahead of schedule. If you'd looked across the landscape, this would have been the only fig tree that would have had fully developed leaves. So the leaves were ahead of time, but the figs were not. You get the idea that Jesus wasn't really making a big deal of this. He was talking to the tree. And the disciples just happened to be close enough to hear. Wow, look at that. Why would he do that? Well, we're not given complete insight into this, but I think it was a combination of things. First, consider Christ's condition He's in the last week of his ministry. The established religious leaders were surely out to kill him. Relationally, one of his insiders was about to betray him, and all of his followers were going to scatter like dust. Spiritually, he's about to suffer the weight of every sin that every believer will ever commit. Physically, he's going to suffer severe agonizing pain, and he knows it's coming. And then his work schedule on top of that includes a whole lot of things that must be accomplished in the next several days. One of them would be clearing the temple. So how do you think you would be approaching life with that weight on your shoulders? It isn't difficult to imagine that Jesus would be a bit short with an object that he knew had no eternal value. Just in his life situation, that would be understandable. Second, the nation of Israel was often compared to a fig tree. Hosea 9. 10, Nahum 3. 12, and Zechariah 3. 10 all compare Israel to a fig tree. And the Old Testament talks about the promise that the nation of Israel held, but it never lived up to its promise. In the case, in this uh text I'm going to read, it refers to the nation as a vineyard, but the imagery still holds up. In Isaiah 5, 1 through 7, it says this. Now let me sing to my well-beloved a song of my beloved regarding his vineyard. My well beloved has a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. There's the expectation. He expected it to bring forth good brick good grapes, but it brought forth wild grapes. With this scripture and more like it, it's very likely that those who heard about the fig tree in the future would immediately think of these passages. And would interpret what Jesus did as as being about more than uh cursing an unproductive piece of growing lumber. They more than likely would have interpreted it with a spiritual meaning. It's not a sure thing, but it's a possibility. Jesus knows what he's going to receive from the nation that God has set apart for himself. He knows what this nation that held so much promise is going to do to him, the Creator, in a few days. Possibly this action by Christ is a foretelling of the state that the nation of Israel will soon be in as a result of never living up to the promise that it held. And the third possible reason that Jesus cursed the fig tree could be that Jesus is simply wanting an example to talk about productive prayer. It isn't like the disciples ask Christ, hey, what was all this about? And Jesus avoided the topic, you know, when he asked them the next day. He's uh He used this example to tell the disciples about the power of prayer, and we'll be looking at that next week. This leads me to believe that Christ had a greater purpose in cursing the fig tree than just making himself feel better. But I don't think I would have wanted to have been there on that day acting frivolously. I doubt Jesus was in the state of mind to be trifled with at this point. But these sellers complicated it by requiring the sacrifice to be purchased from them and then again bumping up the price. This was particularly vexing. Then the fourth problem, he would not allow anyone to carry wares through the temple, the wares carriers. But it'd be the same kind of mentality. We would immediately recognize that as displaying a lack of regard for what the service represents. That attitude would be similar to what was going on here in our text. These people had simply lost touch with who God is and what God's about and what he expects. And we take advantage of that. That's got to tick the devil off. And we can praise God for that. You'll you show us our hearts for what they really are. And you allow us to reorient, to receive the true grace that only comes from you, and to bask And to bathe and to party in that grace And to be so addicted to it that we want everyone to catch the disease Help us, Lord, to submit to you. sermons.title: The Widow's Exploitation
sermons.speaker: Jon Zeigler
sermons.text: There are a bunch of really moving sermons that can be preached from this passage. We could talk about the value of sacrificial giving. About faith, about trusting God to take care of you, about how little we usually sacrifice when we give. But look at our text in context Do you see Jesus teaching any of those things? I was prepared to give a sermon about the proper attitude in giving. But that's not what the context is about, which leads me to believe that Jesus was not singling out this woman for her virtue. Look at our context. This is the passage before our text. It says in Matthew 12 or Mark 12, 38 through 40. Then he said to them in his teaching, Beware of the stribes who desire to go around in long robes. Love greetings in the marketplaces the best seats in the synagogues and the best places at feasts, who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers, these will receive greater condemnation. Now look at what that says about how the scribes cheat widows. They come up with spiritual reasons to exploit the widows. That's what we're told Then look at what comes after our text in Mark 13, 1 through 2. Then as Jesus went out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, Teacher, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here. And Jesus answered and said to him, Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone shall be left upon another that shall not be thrown down. Given the context, we can see that Jesus is talking about the condemnation that is soon to fall on this bankrupt religious system. The context is the corruption of a system and Jesus warning his disciples against that The scribes are going to be judged and condemned because of their corruption, which is best displayed by how they treat the powerless. Then he goes on to say after our text that the very building that this woman was giving money to support was going to be torn down stone from stone. It'd be completely destroyed. Now the question comes, do we really think that Christ would have wanted this woman, trusting this corrupt system to the place where she was throwing into it everything that she needed to live off of? Do we think that Christ would have advised her to do such a thing in support of a building that God Himself would oversee the destruction of in a few short years? Now look at our text. Does Jesus make a single statement telling the disciples what a wonderful thing this woman did? Did he say anything about her faith? Did he tell them that they should follow her example? Did he even say it's a good example to follow? Christ doesn't even say that this woman is a follower of his. There is nothing in the context that tells us that what this woman did was good or wise or exemplary. All we know is that it was sacrificial. She gave everything that she had. And who did she give it to? A self-serving, corrupt religious system that demanded much from people and gave them little in return. After looking at the context and the context, uh the text and the context, I believe the topic is not how to be an exemplary giver. I think the topic is really how to avoid being a religious sucker. Another title for the sermon would be The Danger of Being an Undiscerning Follower. I wanted to use this sermon to encourage sacrificial giving. After all, this church has bills to pay. It pays me. And we may need a small loan to finish construction on the building. Fortunately, we have cheap help. And most of the sermons I've heard on this text make this woman a patron saint on giving. Now it's true that God loves a cheerful giver, and it's our obligation to pay for the services we receive from being part of this church, but this is not the passage that will preach that sermon. So I was kind of disappointed. Let's look at our text. Verse 41. Now Jesus sat opposite the treasury and saw how the people put money into the treasury, and many who were rich put in much. Okay, Jesus sat in the court of the women. This was open to everyone. Evidently there were thirteen trumpet-shaped receptacles into which people placed their offerings. The New Testament, the New International Greek Testament tells us this about the gifts in the temple. It says, the objects for which the money was given Apart from the two chests for the temple tax, so you have two two chests that were used for the temple tax are listed in the Mishnah as bird offerings, young birds for whole offerings, wood, incense. Gold for the caparet, perhaps sacred vessels, and free will offerings, six chests being devoted to the last. All contributions were therefore for the work of the temple. Charitable donations for the poor were made separately. So this lady was giving for the work of the temple. John MacArthur says this, it must have deeply grieved and angered Christ to see people sacrificing their money to this wretched, apostate, corrupt system of false religion. under the misguided assumption that doing so would please God and produce divine blessings. I guess the most dangerous idea Was that giving money to the system was somehow pleasing to God and maybe earning the giver something special with God I've heard a lot of health and wealth preachers teach the same sort of thing. They somehow make the point that giving money to their ministry Win some kind of special favor with God, some special blessing, some inside track. What a horrible lie But it's commonly used to succor people who have bad theology to give their hard-earned money One of the worst lies that our enemy has in his arsenal is that there are things that we can do that will earn favor with God. The idea that we can do something that will create an obligation with God toward us is a deadly kind of evil that allows people to exploit us in the name of God. They'll say, give this money and do this thing or pray this prayer. And now God is obligated to do this thing for you. And somehow the so-called minister always finds a way to profit from providing this power to God for us. Maybe this uh this woman giving her last pennies believed that by doing so she was winning favor with God. Maybe the scribes had told her that if she hopes to have any chance for heaven, she had better put up some cash. We don't know. But not much has changed. Today we see that Ken Copeland needs a jet to minister for God. Now, where do you think the money came to buy it? You can rest assured that some of the funds for that jet have come from some poor widow somewhere given what she couldn't afford to give. The same kind of exploitation is happening today as what happened in Jesus' day. Undiscerning people are being fooled into thinking that they can get what they want from God by doing certain things, by giving certain gifts. by earning certain rewards. And it is just as evil as what the Sadducees were doing in Jesus' day. As Christ was watching, the people putting their gifts into the receptacles in the temple, he noticed this, and many who were rich put in much. So, you know, you'd have your name under the gift that you gave. The Romans looted all these things when they destroyed the temple. So the rich gave a lot because they probably thought they were buying favor with God, and at the same time they were gaining influence for themselves. There was a plaque honoring their spirituality. So when the rich gave, they sort of gave and they sort of got They might be giving something up, but they're achieving something for themselves in their gifts. Some notoriety. They're lofting up their own names. Now, the crime is not so great when the rich give up their abundance, because they're giving something that they could afford to give up. Something else we need to look at is the word rich in Scripture. It means someone who is fully supplied and has enough. Someone who is fully supplied and has enough. Question comes down, are you rich? And all of us would say, well, no, I'm not rich. That's funny. You you gotta see what I drive. But the question is, are you fully supplied and do you have enough? Who here isn't rich? By that by that definition, who isn't rich? When have any of us gone without a meal because we couldn't afford it? How much food do we have in our cupboards? We don't need to feel guilty for it, but we need to see ourselves from a biblical perspective, we are rich. We can give a lot and still not suffer for what we have given. But look at verse 42. Then one poor widow came and threw in two mites, which makes a quadrant. There's a lot contained in that one verse. This coin is 164th of a day's wages. 164th of a day's wages. So say eighty-eight dollars is a day's wage for us, just just throwing in a $11 an hour kind of deal. This coin would be $1. 38. That's essentially in our value what it would be. He sees this happen and he does this next thing. Verse 43. So he called his disciples to himself and said to them, Assuredly I say to you that this poor widow is put in more than all those who have given to the treasury. For they all put in out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all that she had, her whole livelihood. Now, notice who the person is. She is a poor widow. These are the very people who the scribes exploit. That's the very people that were told over and over again that God gets really angry when they are exploited. The word for poor here means the poorest of the poor. Why is Jesus pointing this out? My guess is that he was reorienting their thinking. They may well have thought, the disciples may well have thought that those who gave the most were the most impressive. maybe even the most spiritual. But Jesus is showing, what he's showing is that when regarded from a heavenly perspective, a true perspective, the poor woman gave the most. Why? Because it's a matter of percentages. She gave 100%. She gave all she had to live on. The religious big shots, the ones making all the rules, the ones pretending to be awesome and great and benevolent, the ones who are getting all the benefits are only given a small percentage of what they own. And they probably feel like they're the ones who are morally superior. They're probably the ones who portray themselves as being the morally superior, because look how much they gave. But that isn't true. The most sincere follower, the most devoted follower, the most generous contributor is the poor woman who cannot even afford the gift that she has given. I think the point is all these big shots haven't really given anything of significance. Yet they expect the demands of their religion to be fair. But those people who accept the demands of the religion are the ones who suffer the most. Because the poor give up all they have and all they need in the vain hope that their sacrifice will please God.
